items.title: India's 'own GPS', which new ISRO satellite can restore
items.syllabus: GS3 › Awareness in the field of space; Indigenisation of technology and developing new technology; Security challenges and their management in border areas · GS4 › Foundational values: courage of conviction, fortitude
items.summary: ISRO is launching NVS-03 to restore NavIC, India's regional navigation system, which stopped giving location data after repeated satellite failures.
ideas: Strategic sovereignty in space: NavIC (the working name of IRNSS) is a seven-satellite system covering India and up to 1,500 km around it. India is the only country with a regional navigation system; the four global ones are GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou.
GS3 · Space / strategic autonomy
NavIC gives India its own positioning, navigation and timing, so it need not depend on foreign systems such as GPS in a crisis.

Serving citizens and soldiers: when fully working, NavIC gives the public accuracy of up to 10 metres and a restricted, fee-based service to users such as the military. It covers the Indian landmass better than GPS, whose signals reach India at an angle and struggle in valleys and forests.
GS3 · Dual-use technology / border security
As a dual-use system, NavIC serves both public navigation and the armed forces, with better coverage in India's valleys and forests than GPS.

Imported parts were the weak link: six of the 11 navigation satellites launched since 2013 failed, mainly because of defective imported atomic clocks. Replacements also failed: IRNSS-1H's heat shield did not open and NVS-02's propulsion failed. The Centre told Parliament this year that the system no longer gave position data.
GS3 · Indigenisation / critical components
NavIC's failures show that a strategic system is only as sovereign as its least indigenous component.

Learning from failure: from NVS-01, satellites carry Indian-made atomic clocks with a 12-year life (up from 10), and propulsion systems now get more thorough checks. The new L1 frequency, the band GPS mostly uses, lets NavIC work with other systems and run on low-power chips in smartwatches.
GS3 · Indigenisation · GS4 · Learning organisation
By building its own atomic clocks and tightening checks after failures, ISRO turned setbacks into a stronger second generation of NavIC.
keywords: The three services a navigation system gives
Strategic autonomy in PNT is as vital as autonomy in energy or defence.
Reliance on imports for parts a system cannot work without
Critical component dependence, as with NavIC's imported atomic clocks, can ground an entire strategic system.
Ability to work alongside other systems
Adding the L1 band makes NavIC interoperable with GPS and usable in everyday devices.
Technology serving both civilian and military needs
NavIC is dual-use: a public utility in peace and a strategic asset in conflict.
Risk of a foreign system being switched off or degraded in a crisis
An indigenous system guards against signal denial during conflict.
Coverage limited to a region rather than the whole world
India chose a regional system, giving it focused coverage at a fraction of a global constellation's cost.
examples: Defective imported clocks caused most of NavIC's satellite failures
NavIC's imported atomic clocks failing is a textbook case of strategic risk from critical imports.
New-generation satellites add the L1 band used by low-power wearable chips
With the L1 band, NavIC reaches everyday devices such as smartwatches.
After clock, heat-shield and propulsion failures, ISRO built clocks at home, tightened checks and launched again
ISRO's return to launch after repeated failures shows institutional courage: owning mistakes and persisting.
pyqs: The advantage India saw in IRNSS: an independent regional system; the NavIC setbacks test that promise.
Why India needs IRNSS: sovereignty, better coverage of the Indian landmass, security.
Space applications for socio-economic development: navigation for transport, fisheries, disaster management.

trend.t: UPSC first asked about navigation directly: the advantage of IRNSS over GPS (GS3 2015) and why India needs IRNSS (GS1 2018). Later space questions moved to specific missions: a space station (2019), Chandrayaan-3 (2023) and Mission Drishti (2026).
trend.watch: IRNSS has been asked twice, in two different papers (GS3 2015, GS1 2018). Navigation is a must-study area, now with the failures and the indigenous fix.
focus: Need for and advantages of NavIC over GPS
Civil and military uses of NavIC
Recent ISRO missions and their objectives

potential: NavIC's setbacks highlight the risks of dependence on imported critical components in strategic technologies. Discuss, and suggest measures to strengthen India's space-based navigation capability. (15 marks)
Why does India need its own regional navigation system when global systems such as GPS are freely available? Explain. (10 marks)
What changes have been made in the second generation of NavIC satellites, and how do they improve the system's usefulness? (10 marks)

practice.q: Why does India need its own regional navigation system when global systems such as GPS are freely available? Explain.

answer.t: NavIC, the seven-satellite Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System, makes India the only country with its own regional navigation system.

pts.t: Foreign systems can be switched off or degraded in a conflict; an indigenous system removes this signal-denial risk.
A restricted, encrypted service supports the armed forces in guidance, troop movement and border surveillance.
pts.ex: NavIC's fee-based restricted service for select users.

pts.t: GPS signals reach India at an angle and weaken in valleys and forests; NavIC is designed for the Indian landmass.
pts.ex: Accuracy up to 10 metres for public use.

pts.t: Precise positioning helps rescue operations and guides fishermen at sea.
Transport, logistics, surveying and large construction projects need reliable positioning.
Building satellites and indigenous atomic clocks strengthens India's space industry.
pts.ex: Indian-made atomic clocks from NVS-01 onwards.

pts.t: Learn from the imported clock failures; build key components at home.
Plan replacements ahead of satellites' end of life.
Encourage NavIC-enabled chips in phones and wearables through the L1 band.

answer.t: A fully restored NavIC would turn India's space capability into everyday strategic security.

items.title: The geography & economy of Punjab's long drug crisis
items.syllabus: GS3 › Linkages of organised crime with terrorism; Security challenges in border areas; Role of external state and non-state actors · GS2 › Issues relating to health; Government policies and interventions · GS1 › Social issues: youth, women · GS4 › Probity in governance
items.summary: An anti-drug activist's killing and a recent overdose death have put Punjab's 15-year drug crisis back at the centre of politics ahead of next year's Assembly elections.
ideas: Geography makes Punjab vulnerable: its 553-km border with Pakistan lies on the route from the Golden Crescent (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran). Police officers call Pakistan's pushing of drugs into Punjab after militancy faded 'narco-terrorism'.
GS3 · Border security / narco-terrorism
Punjab's 553-km border with Pakistan places it on the Golden Crescent route, turning drug trafficking into a security threat.

Supply from all directions: heroin (chitta) comes across the border, opium and poppy husk from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh (where cultivation is legal for medical use), charas from Himachal Pradesh, and pharmaceutical drugs from manufacturing hubs in neighbouring states.
GS3 · Organised crime · GS2 · Centre-state coordination
Drugs reach Punjab from across the border and from neighbouring states, so the fight needs coordination among states, not only border policing.

The problem shifts when pressed: as border enforcement improved, abuse of pharmaceutical drugs rose sharply, and smugglers turned to drones, mostly small Chinese quadcopters dropping heroin and arms, often in daylight.
GS3 · Technology and security
Each crackdown has shifted the trade to a new route, from heroin to pharma drugs and from land to drones.

Social and economic roots: opium had social acceptance even before Independence; a single run as a drug mule can earn about a lakh where jobs lag aspirations; easy, underhand wealth is increasingly accepted; whole families, including women, are drawn in.
GS1 · Youth / women · GS3 · Unemployment
Unemployment and social acceptance of easy money feed both addiction and the trade, making it a social as much as a security problem.

Enforcement first, prevention later: governments have followed the EDP model (Enforcement, De-addiction, Prevention), from a 'war on drugs' (2014) and supply crackdowns (2022) to Yudh Nasheyan Virudh (2025), which targeted drug money and moved to community action with 1.5 lakh village volunteers. Drugs remain available; observers say prevention and rehabilitation should come first.
GS2 · Government interventions / health
Enforcement alone has not ended Punjab's drug crisis; prevention and rehabilitation must lead, with enforcement in support.
keywords: Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran: one of the world's three major heroin-processing hubs
Punjab's western border sits on the Golden Crescent route, making it India's frontline against heroin.
Myanmar, Thailand and Laos: the other major heroin-producing region near India
India lies between the Golden Crescent in the west and the Golden Triangle in the east.
Using drugs to weaken a state or fund terror
Drug trafficking across Punjab's border is a form of narco-terrorism, not just crime.
Pressing one supply route pushes the trade to another
The shift from border heroin to pharma drugs shows the balloon effect of supply-only enforcement.
Medicines leaking from legal supply into addiction
Diversion of pharmaceutical drugs calls for tighter regulation of manufacturers and chemists.
Policing the trade versus reducing the need for drugs
A lasting answer must balance supply-side policing with demand-side prevention and rehabilitation.
Following the money hurts trafficking networks more than arresting carriers.
Involving local people in enforcement and prevention
Village volunteers make the anti-drug effort a community movement, not just a police drive.
data: Cases of drug possession for trafficking in Punjab in 2024, the highest in India (Uttar Pradesh next with 3,219)
Punjab recorded 6,060 drug-trafficking possession cases in 2024, the highest in India (NCRB).
Share of India's pharmaceutical drug seizures / heroin seizures in Punjab alone, 2024
Punjab alone accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures and 44% of heroin seizures in 2024.
Drone drops recorded by the BSF, 2021 to 2025
Drone drops on the Punjab border rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025 (BSF).
Rise in arrests of women under the NDPS Act, 2015 to 2022
Arrests of women under the NDPS Act in Punjab rose 85% between 2015 and 2022.
Extension of BSF jurisdiction inland in Punjab, 2021
In 2021 the Centre extended the BSF's jurisdiction from 15 km to 50 km inland.
examples: The BSF set up an anti-drone intelligence wing and Punjab Police bought anti-drone guns, yet smugglers still evade them
Despite anti-drone units, drones still ferry drugs and arms across the Punjab border.
A Punjab Police DSP arrested in a multimillion-rupee drug racket, convicted in 2019
The Bhola case exposes the nexus of traffickers, police and politicians that sustains the drug trade.
Traffickers use women because they are less likely to be searched; some women addicts turn peddlers
Traffickers exploit women as carriers, adding a gender dimension to the drug trade.
Community-driven phase of Punjab's anti-drug campaign
Punjab's 1.5 lakh village volunteers show community participation as part of the fight against drugs.
pyqs: The Golden Crescent next door and the links between drugs, arms and money: the Punjab border is the live case.
Drones ferrying arms and drugs: drone drops rose from 3 (2021) to over 200 (2025).
Narco-terrorism: Pakistan pushing drugs into Punjab after militancy faded.

trend.t: UPSC moved from the links between drug trafficking and other crimes (2018) to the technology that carries drugs, drones (2023), and then to narco-terrorism as a national threat (2024). GS4 also set a case study on a frontier district overrun by narcotics (2019).
trend.watch: Drugs and security have come in GS3 in 2018, 2023 and 2024, and in a GS4 case study in 2019. Narco-terrorism is a must-study area.
focus: Narco-terrorism and the Golden Crescent and Golden Triangle
Drones and technology in border smuggling
Supply-side vs demand-side strategy; de-addiction and rehabilitation

potential: Punjab's drug crisis is as much a socio-economic problem as a security challenge. Critically examine, and suggest a balanced strategy combining enforcement, de-addiction and prevention. (15 marks)
Tighter border enforcement has shifted the drug trade to pharmaceutical drugs and drones. Discuss the challenges this poses and the measures needed. (10 marks)
India lies between the Golden Crescent and the Golden Triangle. Examine the implications for its internal security. (10 marks)

practice.q: Tighter border enforcement has shifted the drug trade to pharmaceutical drugs and drones. Discuss the challenges this poses and the measures needed.
parts: Introduction: the shift in one line, with facts

answer.t: Punjab accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures in 2024, and BSF-recorded drone drops rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025.

pts.t: Pressure on one route pushes the trade to another, so supply-only enforcement keeps chasing the problem.
pts.ex: Heroin to pharma drugs after border tightening.

pts.t: Pharma drugs come from licensed manufacturers and chemists, making them harder to police than contraband.
pts.ex: About 80% enter Punjab from hubs in neighbouring states.

pts.t: Supply comes from several states, but policing is state-wise, leaving coordination gaps.
Small quadcopters drop drugs and arms, often in daylight, and evade detection.
The same drones carry arms, tying drug smuggling to terrorism.
Collusion between traffickers, police and politicians weakens enforcement.
Track sales of habit-forming medicines from manufacturer to chemist.
Layered detection and jamming along the border, with BSF–state police coordination.
Financial investigation to break trafficking networks.
De-addiction, rehabilitation and jobs for youth, with community participation.

answer.t: Only a strategy that cuts both supply and demand can break a trade that adapts faster than enforcement.

items.title: For affordable cancer care, go beyond price caps
items.syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to development and management of health; Government policies and interventions · GS3 › Issues relating to intellectual property rights · GS4 › Ethics in business
items.summary: The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP; the editorial argues the cap alone will not make treatment affordable.
ideas: The cap tackles only the middlemen: it limits the margin on sale to patients, not the price at which companies sell to distributors or hospitals. If that starting price is high, the drug stays unaffordable.
GS2 · Health / regulation
Capping trade margins treats the symptom downstream while the real cost is set upstream by the manufacturer's price.
Patents give pricing power: patented cancer drugs face little generic competition, so manufacturers control prices, and earlier caps on the same drugs did not stop prices from rising.
GS3 · IPR and access to medicines
Where patents shut out generics, price caps on margins cannot discipline the manufacturer's price.
Hidden discounts hide the real price: steep discounts on a few units to select corporate hospitals, with most stock sold higher, make the true market price hard for regulators to know.
GS2 · Regulatory capacity
Selective discounts distort the market price, so margin regulation needs scrutiny of manufacturers' prices and transparent sales data.
A blanket cap can backfire: pharmacies have genuine storage and handling costs; a rigid cap could disrupt supplies to underserved areas, and hospitals may pass costs on through higher room rents.
GS2 · Policy design
A blanket price cap risks shortages in underserved areas and cost-shifting by hospitals.
Price control works only with the health system: stronger public health services, wider insurance coverage and more research on generics must accompany the cap.
GS2 · Universal health coverage
Affordable cancer care needs price regulation backed by public health services, insurance and generics.
keywords: NPPA's tool of capping margins between manufacturer and patient
Trade Margin Rationalisation caps the chain's margin but leaves the manufacturer's price untouched.
Where the cost is set versus where the cap bites
Regulation that targets downstream margins misses upstream pricing power.
When the true market price cannot be known
Selective discounts create price opacity that defeats margin regulation.
Recovering a capped margin through other charges
Hospitals may offset drug caps by cost-shifting to room rents.
Health spending that pushes households into distress
Unaffordable cancer drugs are a leading cause of catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure.
Balancing affordable medicines with incentives for research
Drug pricing policy must balance access with incentives for innovation.
data: Average profit mark-up added by intermediaries (stockists, distributors, hospital pharmacies, wholesalers) on cancer drugs
Intermediaries add an average mark-up of about 170% on cancer drug prices (NPPA).
New cap on the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs
The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP.
Reported monthly cost of the breast cancer drug ribociclib, despite profit restrictions in 2019
Ribociclib's monthly cost reportedly rose from ₹58,000 to ₹78,000 despite 2019 profit caps.
examples: A breast cancer drug whose price rose despite margin caps
Ribociclib shows that margin caps fail when patents leave the manufacturer's price unchecked.
Unaffordable drugs lead patients to delay treatment, skip doses or stop medication
When cancer drugs are unaffordable, patients delay treatment or skip doses, turning cost into lost lives.
pyqs: The State's role against marketisation of healthcare: drug-price regulation is one such tool, with its limits.
Limits of the public health system and the private sector's role: affordable medicines are part of universal coverage.
Section 3(d) and the Novartis case: patents versus access to affordable medicines.

trend.t: Health questions moved from goals and access (MDGs 2013, universal coverage 2015, community-level care 2018) to the State's moral and practical role (primary health 2021) and, most recently, to containing the marketisation of healthcare (2024). In GS3, patents and access to medicines appeared in 2013.
trend.watch: The balance between the State and the private sector in health has come in 2015 and 2024. Regulation of the health market is a must-study area.
focus: State regulation of drug prices and hospital charges
Universal health coverage and out-of-pocket expenditure
Patents, generics and access to medicines

potential: "Regulating trade margins alone cannot ensure affordable access to essential medicines in India." Critically examine. (15 marks)
Discuss the role of intellectual property rights in the pricing of life-saving drugs in India. How can access be balanced with innovation? (10 marks)
Examine the challenges in regulating the prices of medicines in India and suggest measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: Examine the challenges in regulating the prices of medicines in India and suggest measures.
parts: Introduction: the price cap in one line, with facts

answer.t: The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP, where intermediaries added an average 170% mark-up (NPPA).

pts.t: Margin caps do not cover the manufacturer's price to distributors and hospitals.
pts.ex: Ribociclib's cost rose from ₹58,000 to ₹78,000 despite 2019 caps.

pts.t: Patented drugs face little generic competition, so prices stay high.
Selective discounts to corporate hospitals hide the real market price.
Hospitals may recover capped margins through room rents and other charges.
Rigid caps may make supply to underserved areas unviable for pharmacies.
Low insurance coverage leaves patients paying out of pocket.
pts.ex: Patients delay treatment or skip doses.

pts.t: Mandatory reporting of sales and discounts.
More research on and production of generic versions.
Strengthen public hospitals and coverage for cancer care.
Allow for legitimate storage and handling costs.

answer.t: Price caps can lower bills, but only a strong public health system can make cancer care truly affordable.

items.title: Siang dam: Why the project to counter China faces opposition in Arunachal
items.syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood: relations; Bilateral agreements affecting India's interests; Effect of policies and politics of other countries on India's interests
items.summary: India's 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, meant to counter China's 60,000 MW upstream dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo, faces protests from the local Adi community.
ideas: Hydro-hegemony: China, the upstream power on the Yarlung Tsangpo (the Siang in India), approved a 60,000 MW project in December 2024. India, downstream, fears China could release water at will; India's 11,200 MW Siang project is pitched as a counter, and experts say India has a right to details of China's project.
GS2 · India–China / water as a strategic tool
Upstream control of the Brahmaputra lets China practise hydro-hegemony, making transboundary rivers a new front in India–China relations.

Domestic factors shape foreign policy: the Siang project's strategic logic runs into local resistance over ancestral land, livelihood and culture; experts say it cannot go ahead without the local community's cooperation.
GS2 · Domestic factors in foreign policy
The Siang protests show that India's external strategy depends on domestic consent: foreign policy begins at home.
keywords: Using upstream control of a river for power over downstream states
China's mega-dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo raises fears of hydro-hegemony over the Brahmaputra.
The leverage an upstream state has over water flowing downstream
As the upper riparian, China holds leverage over India's Brahmaputra flows.
Leaders must satisfy both foreign counterparts and domestic constituencies
The Siang project is a two-level game: countering China abroad while winning local consent at home.
examples: Local residents in Arunachal's Siang belt oppose the dam over loss of ancestral land and livelihood
Adi protests against the Siang dam show how local concerns can complicate a strategic project aimed at China.
pyqs: Domestic factors influencing foreign policy: the Siang protests are a fresh India–China example.

ethics.title: The courage to try again
ethics.news: After repeated satellite failures grounded NavIC, ISRO built its own atomic clocks, tightened checks and is launching again.
ethics.syllabus: Foundational values for civil service: courage of conviction, fortitude · Leadership
ethics.link: Institutions show courage when they own failure openly, fix its causes and persist, instead of abandoning hard missions to avoid blame.
ethics.question: "In public service, the fear of failure can be more harmful than failure itself." Discuss with examples.

ethics.title: When guardians join the trade
ethics.news: Punjab's drug trade is sustained partly by a nexus of traffickers, police and politicians, exposed in the 2013 Bhola case.
ethics.syllabus: Probity in governance · Integrity and conflict of interest
ethics.link: When enforcers collude with offenders, laws lose their force and public trust collapses; integrity of the enforcer is the first line of defence.
ethics.question: As SP of a border district, you find some of your own staff protecting drug peddlers. What steps will you take, and how will you restore public trust?

ethics.title: Profit on a life-saving drug
ethics.news: Intermediaries add an average 170% mark-up on cancer drugs; the government has capped the seller's profit at 30% of the MRP.
ethics.syllabus: Ethics in business and medicine · Compassion towards the weaker sections
ethics.link: When profit on life-saving medicines pushes patients to skip doses, business ethics demands that access to treatment come before margins.
ethics.question: "Life-saving medicines are a matter of right, not a market commodity." Examine the ethical issues in drug pricing.

ethics.title: Slow, but never stopping
ethics.news: The Editorial Page's Wordly Wise: "It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop" (commonly attributed to Confucius).
ethics.syllabus: Contributions of moral thinkers · Foundational values: dedication to public service, perseverance
ethics.link: Reform in governance is slow; a civil servant's dedication shows in persisting through delay and setback rather than giving up.
ethics.question: "It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop." What does this quotation convey to you in the context of public service?

ethics.title: Comparison as a loop
ethics.news: A mother of two teenagers writes how social media turns comparison into a loop of envy, and how to break it.
ethics.syllabus: Attitude: social influence and persuasion · Emotional intelligence · Role of family in inculcating values
ethics.link: Feeds that compare curated highlights with unfiltered lives shape attitudes; families that motivate by comparison pass the habit on, and self-awareness breaks the loop.
ethics.question: "Social media has turned comparison from an occasional act into a constant habit." Discuss its ethical implications and the role of family in building a healthy sense of self among the youth.

ethics.title: When corruption costs power
ethics.news: A student-led movement in Serbia, sparked by a deadly canopy collapse seen as a symbol of alleged corruption, won elections and unseated the President after over a decade.
ethics.syllabus: Corruption and probity in governance · Accountability
ethics.link: Corruption erodes public trust until citizens demand accountability; a peaceful, organised movement turned that anger into political change.
ethics.question: "Unchecked corruption ultimately erodes the legitimacy of those in power." Discuss with examples.

essay.title: Failing forward: ISRO and NavIC
essay.text: Six of the 11 navigation satellites ISRO launched since 2013 failed: imported atomic clocks broke down, a heat shield did not open, a propulsion system failed. ISRO did not abandon NavIC. It built atomic clocks at home, tightened its checks and is launching again. The cost of doing wrong is smaller than the cost of doing nothing.
essay.use: For 'A ship in harbour is safe, but that is not what ship is for' (2022) and 'Courage to accept and dedication to improve are two keys to success' (2019).

essay.title: Slow, but never stopping
essay.text: "It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop." (commonly attributed to Confucius). Bridging line: nations, like individuals, are built not by sprints but by unbroken stride.
essay.use: As an opener or closer for essays on perseverance and incremental change, e.g. 'Courage to accept and dedication to improve are two keys to success' (2019).

essay.title: The great leveller in reverse
essay.text: A mother of two teenagers writes that social media makes us compare others' curated highlights with our own unfiltered lives. Quoting James Clear, 'Comparison is useful as a point and destructive as a loop.' Her answer: name the comparison, curate the feed, treat others' success as a mirror, and measure yourself against who you were yesterday.
essay.use: For 'Social media is Triggering Fear of Missing Out amongst the youth' (2024), 'The process of self-discovery has now been technologically outsourced' (2021) and 'Social media is inherently a selfish medium' (2017).

essay.title: Serbia: from a canopy collapse to a change of government
essay.text: In November 2024 a canopy collapsed at Novi Sad railway station in Serbia, killing 16. It became a symbol of alleged corruption and lack of accountability. Students began with campus assemblies and blockades; teachers, farmers and actors joined. In two years their 'Student List' won 141 of 250 seats, peacefully unseating President Vučić after over a decade in power.
essay.use: For 'With greater power comes greater responsibility' (2014) and 'Nearly all men can stand adversity, but to test the character, give him power' (2024).
